facts.claim: UNESCO lists 'Samba de Roda of the Recôncavo of Bahia' (Brazil), inscribed in 2008 (3.COM) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity (originally proclaimed in 2005). UNESCO describes it as music, dance and poetry, a popular festive event that developed in the Recôncavo region of Bahia in the seventeenth century, drawing on the dances and traditions of the region's enslaved Africans and on Portuguese elements.

UNESCO says the Samba de Roda is performed on various occasions, such as popular Catholic festivities or Afro-Brazilian religious ceremonies, and also in more spontaneous settings; everyone present, including beginners, is invited to join; participants gather in a circle (roda). UNESCO's text does NOT mention weddings, so the article may only present it as music couples may choose for a celebration, not as a wedding custom.

UNESCO lists 'Frevo, performing arts of the Carnival of Recife' (Brazil), inscribed in 2012 (7.COM) on the Representative List. UNESCO describes it as music and dance performed mainly during the Carnival of Recife, with a quick, vigorous rhythm played by bands and fanfares; the dance is called 'Passo'. UNESCO's text links it to carnival, not weddings or private celebrations: mention only as regional music a couple may choose, no wedding claim.

CNJ Resolution No. 175 of 14 May 2013 (status: Vigente, in force) provides that competent authorities may not refuse the habilitação, celebration of civil marriage, or conversion of a stable union into marriage between people of the same sex (art. 1); a refusal must be reported immediately to the supervising judge (art. 2).

Priberam dictionary defines 'bem-casado' (masculine noun) as a small cake of soft sponge made from eggs and wheat flour, composed of two halves (definition truncated in the page summary read; the related entry 'casadinho' describes two biscuits joined by a sweet filling such as compote, doce de leite or jam, and cross-refers to bem-casado). Spelling with hyphen confirmed: bem-casado.
facts.conflicts: Only the page's meta description (truncated) and the casadinho cross-reference were readable; the filling and wrapping detail for bem-casado itself is not confirmed by this source.

facts.claim: Smartraveller (DFAT), page last updated 1 October 2026: a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) is a DFAT document issued in support of an intended marriage overseas, for when local authorities ask you to prove you are not already married. DFAT issues CNIs through Australian Passport Offices in Australia, through Australian embassies, high commissions and consulates overseas, and by mail. At least one partner must be an Australian citizen or permanent resident.

Smartraveller (DFAT): DFAT charges fees for CNI and notarial services (fees rise with CPI on 1 January each year) and the fee is paid when the application is submitted. A fee applies; no amount to be stated in the article.

Smartraveller (DFAT): DFAT cannot advise on another country's legal processes; couples must confirm with the local authority (or that country's embassy in Australia) whether they need a CNI at all (some accept a Single Status Certificate or No Record Result Certificate from a state or territory births, deaths and marriages registry), whether it must be issued in the country of marriage (if so, the Australian embassy or consulate there can issue it), whether it needs an apostille or authentication, and what other documents are needed (e.g. birth certificate, divorce certificate, deceased partner's death certificate).

Smartraveller (DFAT): the CNI form must be signed in front of an authorised witness (in Australia, e.g. a Justice of the Peace or an Australian Passports official; overseas, a consular official). Supporting documents not in English need an English translation by a professional translator. Incomplete requests cannot be processed, and checks with issuing authorities can cause delays.
